interactions.summary: A student offers a shoulders-of-giants metaphor, Jiang rejects it in favor of birth, and the class confirms that Dante's attachment to Virgil continues past Inferno.

Jiang extends the birth metaphor into a theory of reading Virgil, maps the three canticles onto prophecy, pilgrimage, and revelation, then opens the afternoon session by correcting his earlier account of angelic free will.

claims.claim: Jiang says Inferno's exit should be read as birth: Virgil carries Dante from darkness into light and thereby makes Dante into his symbolic son.
A student notes that Dante later misses Virgil, and Jiang accepts that as evidence that the attachment formed in Inferno persists beyond the escape from hell.
Jiang extends the birth allegory into pedagogy by saying that reading the Iliad in Latin can itself be imagined as Virgil giving birth to the reader.
Jiang says Inferno is prophecy and political criticism, Paradiso is vision and revelation, and Purgatorio therefore has to function as pilgrimage or journey away from Virgil and toward Beatrice.
Jiang corrects his earlier statement by saying Lucifer cries not because he is conscious but because all beings long for God and permanent distance from God is eternal unhappiness.
Jiang explicitly says his morning claim was wrong and replaces it with the view that angels have perfect free will, meaning perfect obedience to God.

signature_moments.moment: Inferno's escape becomes an image of birth: Virgil hauls Dante from total darkness into light and thereby fathers him.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is the packet's sharpest compression of Jiang's Virgil-as-tempter reading and gives the transition into Purgatorio its emotional logic.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang reverses himself in public and defines perfected freedom as obedience rather than unconstrained choice.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It marks a live doctrinal correction that matters for the rest of the lecture's Satan-and-angel reasoning.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's corrected formulation that freedom reaches perfection as complete obedience to God rather than rebellion.

chronology_notes.note: The lecture crosses a session boundary here: Jiang closes the morning by mapping the whole Divine Comedy, then reopens the afternoon by issuing a direct correction on angelic free will and Lucifer's tears.

uncertainty_notes.note: The transcript says Iliad where the Virgil frame may imply a broader classical-reading point; the packet keeps Jiang's wording without normalizing it.
